title: Vestibular Nerve Section
linked_topic: Ablative and Hearing-Preserving Vestibular Surgery (Labyrinthectomy, Vestibular Neurectomy)
source_label: Cummings 7e (Surgery for Vestibular Disorders) and Pasha 6e
indications: Disabling episodic vertigo from a lateralized unstable peripheral vestibular disorder, usually Ménière disease, in an ear with hearing that the patient considers useful, after medical therapy and usually intratympanic therapy have failed. It selectively divides the vestibular fibers while keeping the cochlear nerve, with vertigo control of about 80 to 95 percent. It needs a craniotomy, so it has higher risk than labyrinthectomy; it does not stop the hearing loss or tinnitus of ongoing hydrops. Approaches are retrosigmoid (most common today), retrolabyrinthine, combined retrolabyrinthine-retrosigmoid, or middle fossa.
setup: Supine or lateral with head turned and pinned or taped; facial nerve EMG and ABR or direct eighth-nerve monitoring
Neuroanesthesia with mannitol and mild hyperventilation; consider lumbar drain
Craniotomy set, otologic drill, microscope, microsurgical scissors and hooks, nerve stimulator
Abdominal fat and fascia available for closure and sealing of mastoid air cells
Contrast MRI reviewed; confirm laterality with audiogram and caloric tests
landmarks: Sigmoid sinus, posterior semicircular canal, endolymphatic sac (retrolabyrinthine)
Cerebellar flocculus overlying the eighth nerve
Trigeminal nerve and tentorium superiorly; CN IX and X inferiorly
Cleavage plane between vestibular (superior) and cochlear (inferior) fibers of CN VIII
Facial nerve anterior to CN VIII; AICA loop
Middle fossa: Bill bar, superior and inferior vestibular nerves in the lateral IAC
danger: Facial nerve and nervus intermedius anterior to the eighth nerve
Cochlear fibers and labyrinthine artery (hearing loss)
Sigmoid sinus and posterior fossa dura
CSF leak through opened mastoid cells
steps: Select the patient and approach

Confirm unilateral vestibular disease with useful hearing on that side, a stable or normal other ear, and that symptoms are unstable spells rather than poor compensation. Choose retrosigmoid for simplicity and speed, retrolabyrinthine when the surgeon wants a transtemporal route, or middle fossa for the most selective division in the lateral IAC.
Retrosigmoid craniotomy

Through a curved postauricular incision, expose the asterion and make a craniotomy behind the sigmoid sinus and below the transverse sinus. Wax any opened mastoid cells. Open the dura in a flap based on the sigmoid sinus.
Retrolabyrinthine alternative

For the retrolabyrinthine route, perform a mastoidectomy, decompress the sigmoid sinus and the dura 1.5 cm behind it, skeletonize the labyrinth, and expose the endolymphatic sac down to the jugular bulb. Incise the presigmoid dura parallel to the sinus and tack it forward.
Release CSF and expose the CPA

Gently retract the cerebellum and open the arachnoid over the cerebellopontine angle cistern to release CSF and relax the brain. Retract the flocculus if needed to see the eighth nerve complex. Identify the trigeminal nerve and tentorium above and the lower cranial nerves below for orientation.
Identify the facial nerve

Find the facial nerve anterior and slightly inferior to the eighth nerve and confirm it with electrical stimulation, which often needs slight retraction of the eighth nerve. Keep the stimulus current low and track facial EMG throughout.
Find the vestibulocochlear cleavage plane

Look for the faint septum or small vessel between the vestibular fibers (superior half, grayer) and cochlear fibers (inferior half, whiter) in the cisternal eighth nerve. In the retrosigmoid approach, drilling a little posterior IAC wall can expose the separated nerves more distally if the plane is unclear.
Divide the vestibular fibers

Separate the superior half along the cleavage plane and cut it sharply with microscissors, keeping the cochlear fibers, nervus intermedius, and facial nerve intact. Avoid cautery near the nerve and protect the AICA loop and labyrinthine artery.
Middle fossa variant

Through a temporal craniotomy, elevate the dura and skeletonize the IAC. Open its dura, confirm the facial nerve by stimulation in the superior compartment anterior to Bill bar, avulse and divide the superior vestibular nerve, then divide the inferior vestibular nerve while protecting the cochlear nerve and labyrinthine artery.
Monitor hearing during section

Watch ABR or direct eighth-nerve action potentials as the fibers are divided. A drop in the signal suggests cochlear fiber or blood supply compromise; stop, irrigate with warm saline, and reassess the plane before cutting more.
Watertight closure

Irrigate the angle and close the dura watertight, adding fascia as needed. In the retrolabyrinthine route, block the aditus with fascia and a bone chip to keep graft out of the middle ear and fill the mastoid with abdominal fat. Wax all mastoid air cells and replace the bone flap.
exit_check: Vestibular fibers divided with facial nerve stimulating normally at the brainstem at low threshold
Cochlear potentials preserved; no vascular injury
Dura closed watertight and mastoid cells sealed
postop: ICU or step-down neurologic checks; watch for hematoma, stroke, and CSF leak
Expect acute vertigo for days; short-term antiemetics and early mobilization
Start vestibular rehabilitation; return to usual activity typically over 2 to 4 months
Audiogram at 6 weeks; ongoing hydrops can still cause fluctuating hearing and tinnitus
Treat postoperative headache, which is more common after retrosigmoid craniotomy

early: Facial nerve paresis (highest with middle fossa)

attending_followup: When do you choose vestibular nerve section over labyrinthectomy?
When the affected ear has hearing that is useful to the patient; labyrinthectomy is preferred for nonserviceable hearing because it is more reliable and avoids a craniotomy.
Where are the vestibular fibers in the cisternal eighth nerve?
In the superior (and slightly posterior) half; the cochlear fibers are inferior. The vestibular nerves become distinct only in the lateral IAC.
Which approach has the highest facial nerve risk, and why might it be chosen?
The middle fossa approach, with temporary paresis rates up to about a third; it gives the most selective section because the superior and inferior vestibular nerves are separate in the lateral IAC.
Why does vestibular nerve section not stop hearing loss in Ménière disease?
It removes only vestibular input; the hydrops continues to affect the cochlea, so hearing can still fluctuate and decline.
What is a typical cause of failure after nerve section, and how is it managed?
Incomplete division of vestibular fibers or poor central compensation; start vestibular rehabilitation, and if residual function is proven, consider labyrinthectomy or revision.
